To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

German middle-class mothers reacted more contingenty to their infants’ communicative signals than Nso mothers, that German toddlers recognized themselves in a mirror more often than Nsotoddlers, and that the level of mothers’ contingent responsiveness was one mechanism that explained mirror self-recognition.
the level of mothers’ contingent responsiveness is associated with the level of mirror self-recognition and that this association differs across cultures.
German mothers were more responsive to their infants’ signals than Nso mothers and that the level of contingency was related to toddlers’ self-recognitions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interplay of cultural and individual influences on the development of self-recognition.
the interplay between culture and parenting styles and the development and emergence of the categorical self in early childhood.
the question of whether the development of self-recognition is related to the cultural context of parenting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Nso and German samples differed in their parenting styles and in their children’s self-recognition, but that the relationship between parenting style and self-recognition could only be established for the Nso sample, which was more homogeneous with respect to the cultural context.
the development of a categorical self in infancy and early childhood is influenced by the cultural parenting styles of the mother.
the development of the self in early infancy is a complex and multi-layered process, which is influenced by many variables.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cultural context in which children grow up influences the development of their sense of self.
contingent responsiveness is a parenting style that fosters the development of a categorical self.
the way parents respond to their child’s signals and behavior is important to the child’s development of self-concepts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cultural variations in parenting styles are associated with variations in children’s self-conceptions.
the way parents interact with their infants influences the development of self-recognition.
the development of self-recognition is a social process, which is shaped in the interaction with the caregiver.
